How does kernel choice affect cold-start latency vs steady-state throughput?

transcript:
Header: 2026-02-25 16:00 UTC | Duration 45m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Jared, Priya, Aaron (Quantica)

00:00:04 Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, this is the weekly POC sync — agenda quick recap of the bench results, tuning items, and next steps.
00:00:12 Aaron: yeah thanks, excited to get into the latency numbers, we've been seeing higher TTFTs than we expected.
00:00:18 Maya: cool, Diego you want to kick off with the profiling summary?
00:00:22 Diego: sure, yeah. quick caveat, these are from the dedicated test run we did on the 4090-like pool, sequence mix was 64 to 1024 tokens, and we pushed a bursty arrival pattern to simulate product traffic. also note some of the labels in the profiler swapped model names, so sorry for the noise.
00:00:40 Diego: overarching: TTFT is dominated by the initial kernel load and compilation phase for some of our larger ops, plus obervable jitter from scheduling at the runtime layer. with streaming on, time to first token drops a lot for short responses, but for longer sequences streaming increases CPU overhead slightly because of per-chunk flushes.
00:01:05 Jared: when you say drops a lot, like what numbers? we saw median TTFT around 320ms on your hosted baseline, expected ~150.
00:01:12 Diego: right. for 32-64 token outputs streaming brought median TTFT to ~140-170ms depending on chunk size; non-streaming cold TTFT stayed around 300-350ms due to first token wasm/kernel init overhead.
00:01:26 Priya: is that a cold start issue only? our product has lots of short-lived sessions so cold-start matters.
00:01:31 Diego: it's a mix. cold start (first request after model idle) triggers extra kernel/memory paths; warm (after KV cache primed) is much better. we saw warm p50 ~90-110ms with streaming.
00:01:44 Aaron: hmm ok. what about p95/p99? that is what we care about for UX.
00:01:48 Diego: p95 for the mixed workload was around 420ms; p99 spiked to 1.1s in some runs because of scheduling contention and occasionally fallback to a compatibility kernel during quantized ops.
00:02:02 Maya: that's where kernel choice comes in right, Diego? can you explain the tradeoffs quickly for their team: specialized kernels vs fallback compatibility kernels.
00:02:10 Diego: yep. so our runtime picks fastest kernels based on seq length and hardware. optimized attention kernels (tensor core fused ops) are fastest for 1k+ context but they have a heavier init path. some quantized kernels are smaller memory footprint but sometimes trigger a slower path for certain head dims, so if the model shape doesn't match the optimized codegen, we fall back and pay latency.
00:02:32 Jared: are these the same kernels we saw in the docs, like 'kv-friendly' and 'fast-attn'? some names came through different.
00:02:37 Diego: yes, but the profiler labels are messy — you'll see names like fast_attn_v2 or attn_fallback. Diego: (laughs) profiler loves to rename things.
00:02:45 Priya: practical question: can we pin kernel choices per-deployment so we avoid runtime fallbacks?
00:02:51 Diego: you can. in Dedicated we expose a kernel policy override so you can prefer stable kernels with slightly worse throughput but lower tail latency. also we can lock quantization profile. tradeoff is cost/throughput.
00:03:05 Aaron: and streaming config — what's the recommended chunk size? we tried chunk 64 and 128 and saw different effects.
00:03:12 Diego: small chunk sizes reduce TTFT because first chunk returns faster, but increase per-token CPU overhead; for high-concurrency short outputs we recommend chunk 64, for long generations chunk 256 tends to be more efficient.
00:03:25 Jared: curious about sequence length distribution: we sample 10k requests from prod, and 60% are under 80 tokens, 30% 80-300, 10% >300. does that change your tuning advice?
00:03:37 Diego: yes, with that distribution streaming + small chunk sizes and KV caching for repeated prefixes will help. batching should be tuned to avoid increasing TTFT for short requests; schedule small micro-batches or prefer dynamic batching thresholds.
00:03:50 Maya: to be clear, the knobs we should try this week: enable streaming with chunk 64, pin a stable kernel policy, and run a 1k sample latency sweep with warm and cold windows. Jared is that doable?
00:04:01 Jared: yes we can run that. we'll need the config file though.
00:04:04 Maya: I'll send the config after the call.
00:04:06 Priya: also we saw in our trace that cold-starts correspond to occasional model reloads because of memory pressure. could you advise on keep-alive / instance sizing?
00:04:15 Diego: sure; increase reserved instance capacity or adjust idle timeout — Dedicated lets you set an idle threshold so instances stay warm. there's also an autoscaler policy to keep a min pool size. that will cost more but reduces cold TTFT.
00:04:30 Aaron: what's the delta in cost for keeping a 2-node warm pool vs letting scale-to-zero?
00:04:35 Diego: ballpark depends on GPU type; for our 80/20 split I'd expect roughly 15-25% incremental spend but a big drop in p99. we'll provide a cost estimate in the follow-up.
00:04:47 Jared: ok, on the kernel profiling you mentioned flamegraphs — can you share those?
00:04:51 Diego: yes I'll share. note: the profiling requires a short dedicated run as it instruments kernels — might add noise to latency but gives clear hotspots.
00:04:59 Maya: quick interruption — someone asked about security and data handling for the bench logs. Priya?
00:05:05 Priya: yes we can't send raw customer data. the logs we can produce are anonymized traces and perf counters; we need to ensure no payloads are exported.
00:05:13 Diego: understood — we'll only share perf counters and aggregated traces. we'll scrub inputs in the bench harness.
00:05:19 Maya: good. diving back — Diego, any low-hanging code/runtime flags we can try to reduce p99?
00:05:24 Diego: a couple: 1) pin stable kernels to avoid fallback, 2) increase KV cache prefill so more requests are warm, 3) tweak batching thresholds to avoid over-batching short requests, 4) enable streaming with appropriate chunk size. each reduces tail in different ways.
00:05:38 Aaron: can you prioritize those for us? like order of impact?
00:05:41 Diego: order: KV cache warm > kernel pinning > streaming chunk tuning > batching threshold. KV cache prevents long re-compute; kernel pin avoids fallback spikes.
00:05:50 Jared: regarding KV cache, how much memory overhead does prefill have? we have memory-constrained instances.
00:05:55 Diego: depends on prefix length; we can quantify — it's roughly linear in prefix length times KV entry size. I'll include an estimate in the profiling artifact.
00:06:05 Priya: any notes about quantization causing fallbacks? we saw larger p99 when enabling 4-bit q.
00:06:11 Diego: 4-bit quant helps throughput but some kernels aren't fully supported and trigger a compatibility path. you can pin non-quantized kernels for tail-sensitive paths and use quantization for bulk throughput. we can also try hybrid: quantize some layers only.
00:06:25 Aaron: ok, so practical next steps and who owns what — maybe we list them.
00:06:30 Maya: yep, summary: Diego will run kernel profiling and share flamegraphs and kernel policy recommendations by 2026-03-01; Quantica (Jared) will run 1k-sample latency sweep with config we'll share and return TTFT/p50/p95/p99 by 2026-03-03; Maya will send config and pricing note by 2026-02-27 and schedule the dedicated bench on 2026-03-05.
00:06:52 Jared: sounds good. one more: can we run a streaming vs non-streaming AB on a small subset to validate UX impact?
00:06:59 Diego: yes we can instrument that on the harness. note that streaming changes tokenization boundary behavior a little so please test for hallucination/regression on a few prompts.
00:07:10 Priya: do you have a recommended test prompt set? we prefer a small representative set.
00:07:14 Diego: we'll share a 50-prompt set that's representative of short/medium/long flows.
00:07:19 Aaron: perfect. any blockers?
00:07:21 Jared: none from infra once we get the config.
00:07:24 Maya: ok if no more questions we'll wrap — thanks everyone. we'll follow up with artifacts in the next 48 hours.
00:07:31 Aaron: thanks!
00:07:33 [meeting ends]

Notes: Transcript contains light transcription errors and occasional label noise per Fireflies export conventions. The full profiler and flamegraph artifacts referenced will be shared as links in follow-up email (not embedded).
